notes: Colour clock 3.579545 MHz; 228 clocks x 262 lines = 59736 clocks per frame; 19912 CPU cycles per frame; 76 cycles per line. Frame rate = 3579545/59736 = about 59.92 Hz (broadcast NTSC is 59.94; the console is not locked to it).

Typical layout: 3 lines VSYNC + 37 lines VBLANK + 192 visible + 30 overscan = 262. Many games use 191-200 visible lines and total 262 regardless; the total must stay at 262 (some TVs tolerate 260-264).
Timer idioms: TIM64T 43 for VBLANK (37 lines = 2812 cycles) and about 35-36 for overscan (30 lines = 2280 cycles), then WSYNC; adjust for your loop overhead.

NTSC hue numbers are the reference for most documentation: $1x yellow-gold, $2x orange, $3x red-orange, $4x red-pink, $5x purple, $6x purple-blue, $7x blue, $8x blue, $9x light-blue, $Ax cyan, $Bx green-cyan, $Cx green, $Dx yellow-green, $Ex olive/orange-green, $Fx tan. Approximate names; display varies by TV and emulator palette.

standards.palette: 128 entries, 16 hues x 8 lumas, but hues 0, 1, 14 and 15 are greyscale so only 12 true hues
notes: Colour clock 3.546894 MHz; 228 clocks x 312 lines = 71136 clocks per frame; 23712 CPU cycles per frame; 76 cycles per line; frame rate about 49.86 Hz.

Typical layout: 3 VSYNC + 45 VBLANK + 228 visible + 36 overscan = 312, though many PAL games use only 192-200 visible lines and larger blank areas (the visible height varies per TV; 228 is the maximum conventionally drawn).
Timer idioms: VBLANK 45 lines = 3420 cycles (about TIM64T 53), overscan 36 lines = 2736 cycles (about TIM64T 42); derive the exact value from your own code.
PAL hue numbering differs from NTSC (hues 2-13 carry colour). A NTSC colour table must be remapped; the same byte gives a different colour.
A PAL console can still be fed a 262-line signal (PAL60, below) but many PAL TVs reject it.
PAL console running the NTSC line count (262 lines): same timing code as NTSC, but PAL colour clock (3.546894 MHz) so frame rate is about 59.38 Hz and the PAL colour table applies.
Not all PAL TVs accept 60 Hz PAL; it is common on 1990s-era PAL TVs and modern ones with composite input. Some PAL games ship a '60 Hz' selection for this purpose.
On an NTSC console the NTSC palette applies; the combination 'NTSC 312 lines at 50 Hz' is called NTSC50 in Stella.

standards.palette: 8 colours only; selected by COLUxx bits 3-1, hue bits 7-4 and bit 0 ignored
notes: SECAM consoles use the same timing as PAL (312 lines, 50 Hz). The TIA outputs one of 8 colours chosen by luminance bits 3-1: 0 black, 1 blue, 2 red, 3 magenta, 4 green, 5 cyan, 6 yellow, 7 white (as commonly documented; verify with a SECAM palette test ROM).
Many SECAM-era games reuse the PAL ROM; the colours then collapse onto this 8-colour set, and sprites with the same luma become the same colour, so play-ability may need a dedicated SECAM table.
Stella also has SECAM60 for a SECAM console on a 262-line signal.

There is NO hardware register that reports the TV standard, so software cannot ask whether the console is NTSC or PAL. Common solutions: ship region-specific ROMs; offer a start-up menu choice (for example SELECT toggles 50/60 Hz and the palette); or use a software heuristic. Colour/BW (SWCHB bit 3) is only the console switch, not the TV standard.

Frame structure: sync the frame with timers rather than counting WSYNCs in the vertical blank: write TIM64T at the start of the VBLANK/overscan and run game logic, then wait for INTIM = 0 and WSYNC. Keep the line count per frame constant; derive loop counts from constants such as VBLANK_LINES, KERNEL_LINES, OVERSCAN_LINES defined per standard with DASM IFCONST/IF blocks (e.g. `IF PAL ... ELSE ... ENDIF`).

Use one colour table per standard (NTSC, PAL, optionally SECAM). Define colours by symbolic names (e.g. COL_RED = NTSC $34 / PAL $64) in an include file switched by an assemble-time flag; do not hard-code hue values.

Timing-dependent code (positioning loops, sprite kernels) is in CPU cycles per line (76) and so is identical in NTSC and PAL; what changes is the number of lines and the frame time. Game speed that depends on frame rate (50 vs 60 Hz) should be compensated with a scale factor on speeds/timers.
A PAL cart usually shows more lines; kernels written for 192 lines leave black borders on PAL unless extended to 228. Stella shows the detected scanline count.

Stella command line: -format <NTSC|PAL|SECAM|NTSC50|PAL60|SECAM60|AUTO> sets the display format (the -bs option is the cartridge type). Stella autodetects by line count and by looking at which colours the game uses; wrong detection can be overridden.

SWCHB colour switch detection (bit 3: 1 = colour, 0 = black and white) can be used to select a monochrome-friendly palette (luma only) when the user flips the TV TYPE switch; this is the intended use of that switch.
